He was struck by the animosity directed at the memorial, but also by the fact that many people were not familiar with Odeh’s life and work, as a librarian informed him. “That combination stayed with me,” Rubin told Hyperallergic . “Here was a monument that was simultaneously being attacked and overlooked: a work that remained politically charged enough to attract repeated acts of vandalism, yet had become somewhat invisible to the public around it.” The statue of Alex Odeh outside the Santa Ana Public Library (photo Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register via Getty Images) After consulting with Bendib and Odeh’s eldest daughter Helena, Rubin received their blessing to remove the dove once more, “this time with intention and care,” for the creation of a new, participatory artwork, “ The Stolen Dove .” Over the course of several months, various individuals and organizations can host the dove for events, dinners, and performances. “Instead of remaining fixed in a public square, the dove would become a living, decentralized monument, gathering people around Alex [Odeh]'s life and legacy through conversation, hospitality, and shared responsibility,” Rubin explained. Each participant who hosts the dove will receive a replica of the statue, “a growing flock dispersed across homes and institutions, creating a network of monuments and storytellers.” Alex Odeh was born into a Catholic family in Jifna, Palestine, in 1944. He experienced the Nakba as a child, and later the Israeli occupation of the West Bank in 1967. Odeh immigrated to the US in 1972, receiving a Master’s degree in political science from California State University, Fullerton, where he also taught Arabic and Middle East history. In the early 1980s, he became the West Coast regional director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), a civil rights organization dedicated to fighting anti-Arab stereotypes, discrimination, and hate crimes. As part of his commitment to peace and justice, Odeh was also invested in promoting inter-community dialogue between Muslims, Jews, and Christians. Alex Odeh with his family in 1985 (photo courtesy Helena Odeh) On October 11, 1985, Odeh was killed when a pipe bomb exploded at the offices of the ADC in Santa Ana. Later that day, he was scheduled to speak at a local synagogue during Friday prayer services. Although the FBI and investigative journalists identified members of the Jewish Defense League, a right-wing terrorist group , as possibly responsible for the bombing, no one has ever been arrested for his murder, and the case remains officially unsolved. “The Stolen Dove” made its debut at the Sundance Film Festival in January for the screening of the documentary film Who Killed Alex Odeh? , before traveling to several events in Southern California, beginning with a dinner hosted by Odeh’s daughter Helena and his widow Norma. The dove visited the home of Julie Kasem, daughter of legendary radio personality Casey Kasem, who helped fund the original statue; the residence of artist elin o'Hara slavick; and a Passover seder held by Rabbi Arnold Rachlis, who spoke at the dedication of Bendib’s memorial sculpture in 1994. “We passed around the dove, let people hold it. I didn’t realize how powerful that would be, these feelings of despair and hope,” Rachlis told Hyperallergic . “The Stolen Dove” (2026), first hosting event at the home of Norma and Helena Odeh (photo Zach Morrison, courtesy Jon Rubin and GCAC) This Saturday, July 18, the dove will be hosted at the 839 house gallery in Hollywood for an evening of music, readings, and food . “The project feels urgent because it brings renewed attention to Odeh’s life and legacy, and to the longer history of anti-Arab violence in this country that his assassination has come to symbolize,” Liz Hirsch, co-founder of 839, told Hyperallergic . “It reminds us that occupation and genocide in Palestine are not just things happening ‘over there,’ but are structurally connected to conditions here in the US and beyond.” Artist and curator Joshua Oduga will perform ambient musical pieces, including a reworking of Sabreen’s 1994 song “Jayy al-Hamam (جاي الحمام)” (“The Doves Are Coming”), which borrows text from a poem by Palestinian poet Hussein Barghouti. “I’m interested in what happens when the dove becomes sound,” Oduga told Hyperallergic . There will also be a reading from Odeh’s 1983 book of poems and essays, Whispers in Exile ( Hamasat fil Ghurba ), newly translated by Emily Drumsta. Rubin will then take the dove to the Bay Area and later to Pittsburgh, where he lives and teaches. A public event in Santa Ana organized by the GCAC is also in the works, according to John Spiak, director of the GCAC. When asked if he had any trepidations about safety, Spiak replied: “There are always concerns, but Alex was a peace activist, and his life was taken. There’s no security with any project you do.” Helena Odeh with the dove in December 2025 (photo Patrick Shartzer, courtesy Jon Rubin and GCAC) The dove is scheduled to be reunited with the statue in the fall of 2027, to commemorate the 42nd anniversary of Odeh’s murder. Helena said she hopes the dove can visit her father’s hometown of Jifna in Palestine before that. Rubin hopes that little by little, house by house, hand by hand, the Stolen Dove will reinvigorate and restore Odeh’s legacy once it is returned to its official perch outside the Santa Ana library. “When the dove eventually returns to the monument, hundreds of people will be able to say, ‘I once held that dove,’” Rubin said. “The hope is that the monument returns carrying the memory of all of A bronze dove that vandals once tore from a monument in Santa Ana, California, is traveling again. This time, it is leaving with permission.

The bird belongs to a memorial for Alex Odeh, a Palestinian-American poet, scholar, and civil-rights organizer assassinated in 1985. Artist Jon Rubin has made the recovered dove the center of *The Stolen Dove*, a participatory artwork whose temporary hosts gather around it and keep a replica after it moves on. The project's history and current circuit of visits are covered in Hyperallergic's [A Living Memorial to Palestinian Activist Alex Odeh Takes Flight](https://hyperallergic.com/a-living-memorial-to-palestinian-activist-alex-odeh-takes-flight/).

## Why the dove left the monument

Khalil Bendib, an Algerian-American sculptor, created the Santa Ana memorial in 1994. His figure of Odeh carries a book and the now-traveling bird, joining scholarship with Odeh's work for peace. The statue later drew repeated attacks. Red paint struck it in 1996 and 1997; in 2020, someone removed the dove by force. It was found and restored before Rubin arranged a deliberate removal in December 2025.

Rubin had first seen the work during a 2023 residency at Santa Ana's Grand Central Art Center. He learned that the monument could remain a target while many people in the surrounding community were not familiar with its subject. With approval from Bendib and Odeh's eldest daughter, Helena, Rubin turned that tension into a different kind of memorial: the original dove moves among people, while replicas mark the relationships formed along its route.

Hosts have brought the object into dinners, performances, and religious gatherings. Odeh's family received one visit; artists opened their homes for others; and one stop placed the bird at a Passover meal. The project also appeared at the January 2026 Sundance premiere of the documentary *Who Killed Alex Odeh?*, according to [Hyperallergic's account](https://hyperallergic.com/a-living-memorial-to-palestinian-activist-alex-odeh-takes-flight/).

## Who Alex Odeh was

Odeh was born in Jifna, Palestine, in 1944 and moved to the United States in 1972. At California State University, Fullerton, political science became his graduate field; his later teaching there covered the Arabic language and the region's history. By the early 1980s, he was leading West Coast work for the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee and promoting dialogue among Muslim, Jewish, and Christian communities.

Odeh died in the October 11, 1985 bombing of the committee's Santa Ana offices; the device was a pipe bomb. He had been due to address a synagogue later that day. The murder remains unsolved. The FBI and journalists have treated members of the Jewish Defense League as possible suspects, but nobody has been arrested for the killing, [Hyperallergic reported](https://hyperallergic.com/a-living-memorial-to-palestinian-activist-alex-odeh-takes-flight/).

## Where the project goes next

The dove reached a Hollywood house gallery on July 18 for a program combining food, music, and readings. The gathering included Joshua Oduga's reinterpretation of a Sabreen song based on Hussein Barghouti's poetry, as well as work from Odeh's own *Whispers in Exile* in a new translation by Emily Drumsta.

Plans described to Hyperallergic send the project next toward the Bay Area and Pittsburgh, with another Santa Ana event also under development. Its longer journey points back to the original monument: the dove is scheduled to return in fall 2027. Helena Odeh also hopes it can visit Jifna before that reunion. Each stop adds another group of people who know whose hand the bird came from—and why it left.
